modules.title: Scheduling & virtual memory
modules.description: Understand processes, scheduling, memory, and the boundaries of a sandbox.

lessons.title: Processes & scheduling
lessons.body:
### Separate a program from its execution
A program is stored code. A process is an executing instance with resources and an address space. Threads within a process share parts of that address space.

### Scheduling chooses who runs
A ready process can run; a blocked process is waiting for something. Round-robin scheduling limits each ready process to a time quantum before it returns to the ready queue.

### Measure a policy
Response time, turnaround time, and waiting time capture different aspects of scheduling. State assumptions about arrivals, context-switch cost, and I/O before calculating them.

lessons.title: Virtual memory & isolation
lessons.body:
### Addresses belong to a context
Virtual memory lets processes use virtual addresses that the system maps to physical memory. Page permissions help enforce access boundaries.

### Faults are not always crashes
A page fault can cause the operating system to resolve a mapping or load a page; an invalid access can instead terminate the process.

### This browser lab is a model
The C++ sandbox does not expose native process creation or host system calls. Use it to simulate scheduling and memory algorithms rather than to control the host operating system.

exercises.title: Calculate a round-robin schedule
exercises.prompt: Three processes arrive at time 0 with CPU bursts A=5, B=3, C=1. The initial queue is A, B, C. Use quantum 2, no I/O, and zero context-switch cost. Write the execution timeline and the turnaround time of each process.
hints: A runs from 0 to 2, then B runs from 2 to 4.
A process that finishes does not rejoin the queue.
All arrivals are at 0, so turnaround time equals completion time.
exercises.answer: Timeline: A 0–2, B 2–4, C 4–5, A 5–7, B 7–8, A 8–9. Turnaround: A=9, B=8, C=5. Waiting times: A=4, B=5, C=4. Average turnaround is 22/3 time units.
